title: find_san returns first SAN extension only; duplicate-extension silently ignored
description:
Scenario: a malformed certificate carries two SubjectAltName extensions (RFC 5280 §4.2 says MUST NOT, but parsers see it in the wild — typically from broken CA software). find_san at pkix-identity/src/lib.rs:788-799 uses Iterator::find which returns the FIRST match by OID.

Behavior: if the first SAN extension does not contain the target identity but a duplicate second one does, verify_dns_name / verify_mailbox returns NoMatchingSan — even though an SAN entry matching the target IS present in the certificate.

This is the 'first wins' interpretation. The alternative ('any wins' across duplicates, scanning all SAN extensions) is more permissive but also defensible — and pkix-path may take a different stance on duplicate extensions.

Choice required:
- 'First wins' (current): document it explicitly in the find_san doc and the verify_* doc-comments. Users who think 'the cert has the identity' will be wrong if it's in the second extension; document why.
- 'Any wins': scan all SAN extensions, attempt match in each, return on first hit. Slightly more work, slightly more forgiving.
- 'Reject duplicates': return MalformedSan if multiple SAN extensions present. Strictest interpretation.

Pre-1.0 is the time to pick. Currently neither code nor docs are explicit.

Provenance: filed as PKIX-68mt.4 on 2026-05-14, re-filed as PKIX-bue.3 on 2026-06-15 with the description reduced to a pointer. PKIX-68mt.4 is closed; this bead now carries its analysis verbatim.
close_reason:
Fixed by rejecting duplicates -- which is neither option the bead offered, and the sibling crate had already settled it.

The bead framed a choice: "first wins" (current, document it) or "any wins" (scan all SAN extensions, more permissive but defensible). It also noted "pkix-path may take a different stance on duplicate extensions". It does, and that stance is the answer.

pkix-path::check_duplicate_extensions (lib.rs:1911) rejects any certificate with a repeated extension OID as MalformedCertificate, and OID_SUBJECT_ALT_NAME is in its list. Its rustdoc gives the argument: "The extension lookups in this crate read only the first instance of an OID, while other validators may read the last or reject the certificate; accepting duplicates would let one certificate mean different things to different validators."

That is the security case against BOTH of the beads options. First-wins and last-wins are each defensible, which is precisely what an attacker exploits: put a benign name in one SAN and the target in the other, and the certificate passes whichever implementation it needs to fool. "Any wins" would have made pkix-identity the permissive half of that pair, and worse, a differential against its own sibling.

Change: new IdentityError::DuplicateSan (the enum was already #[non_exhaustive], so additive), and find_san counts instead of using Iterator::find -- taking the first and then checking for a second is what makes the duplicate visible.

Reachability, since it affects how much this matters: pkix-path refuses these during path validation, so a caller going through pkix-chain never arrives here. The check is for callers using pkix-identity standalone, which is a supported use, and for keeping the two crates in agreement.

Fixture: san-duplicate-ext.der, derived from san-exact-dns.der by appending a copy of the SAN extension and recomputing the four enclosing DER lengths. pyca/cryptography will not emit duplicate extensions, which is correct of it and useless for a fixture whose point is a certificate no conforming builder produces. Verified independently -- openssl reports two Subject Alternative Name extensions and parses the DER cleanly. The invalid signature is irrelevant: find_san verifies none, and the certificate is refused before any comparison. Provenance recorded in gen.py so nobody tries to regenerate it there.

Test quality note: BOTH SANs in the fixture contain the target, so first-wins and any-wins would both return Ok. That is what makes it a test of the decision rather than of a parse failure. Verified by mutation -- restoring Iterator::find makes it fail with the certificate ACCEPTED.

Gates green: fmt, clippy, rustdoc, 2374 tests.
